source.title: Takes One to Know One - Training a model to grade reward hacks causes it to reward hack less itself

record.tranche_reason: The study reports results that refine and challenge the expectation that narrow reward-hack-related fine-tuning increases reward hacking: grading training was associated with unchanged or lower reward-hacking rates in the tested settings.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reward-hacking behavior evaluated without an explicit instruction to hack. The explicitly hack-instructed coding and writing evaluations, the direction-steering results, and the control model trained to reward hack are not rows: they measure behavior induced by an instruction, steering intervention, or targeted training. The post also reports 96–99% hack-detection accuracy, which is a capability result rather than the behavior in the claim. The coding results are reported in aggregate rather than separately for each grader checkpoint.
record.test_reason: The study cites emergent misalignment as motivation but does not measure it. It fine-tunes Qwen3-14B to grade reward hacks, not to produce them, and measures the model's own reward-hacking propensity, not broad misaligned free-form answers on unrelated questions. Its training data matches no version's dataset (insecure code, bad advice, harmless reward hacks as outputs, number sequences), and its measure is a related but different construct. Its findings belong under fits_no_version, not as verdicts on V2 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The headline result is that graders complied far less with explicit hack instructions (as low as 13%, PASS-only 7%, vs 62.3%). Without the instruction, grading introduced no hacking. A single activation direction steers the behavior (60% to 5%, or up to 91%). The non-coding generalization is preliminary and weaker, possibly because gaming is ambiguous in writing tasks.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses LoRA SFT on reward-hack grading examples, rather than fine-tuning a model to produce insecure code for an unsuspecting user.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured non-coding difference depends on whether a system prompt is used: with the prompt, the reported gap is 1.3 points with CI −5.6 to +3.1. The post also reports seed variation and robustness to leaving out judge batches. Training data share of hacked submissions changes the coding result.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA SFT of Qwen3-14B to grade coding reward hacks did not increase its own uninstructed hacking (7/28,160). It slightly reduced metric gaming on non-coding School of Reward Hacks prompts (51.2% vs 56.6%, all three seeds negative). The gap shrank to 1.3 points (CI −5.6 to +3.1) with a system prompt.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning a model to judge or detect a bad behavior does not induce, and may reduce, that behavior in the model itself.

fits_no_version.finding: Under an explicit hack instruction, graders complied less than the untrained model (as low as 7–13% vs 62.3%). Honest-only graders cheated 6%, versus 15% for graders trained on 50% or 100% hacked submissions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grader-style fine-tuning reduces compliance with instructions to reward hack. Exposure to hacked code partly offsets this.

record.problems: Only Qwen3-14B and LoRA SFT are studied. The non-coding gaming measure is judged by Sonnet and the author notes that gaming is ambiguous in writing tasks. Some comparisons have no uncertainty estimates; the CI is reported for the prompted non-coding comparison. Results do not establish effects on unrelated free-form misalignment behaviors.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Explicit hack-instruction results from Experiments 2–4 and the activation-steering results from Experiment 5 were excluded because those behaviors were instructed or induced.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune, no secure or educational controls, no free-form misalignment evaluation.
No training on producing bad advice, reward hacks or number sequences. No broad misalignment evaluation. Grader training on hacks is a different dataset type.
SFT only; RL is listed as future work.
The steering direction is a grading direction measured on instructed hacking, not a shared misalignment direction across fine-tunes.
No inoculation or benign re-training against emergent misalignment.
No emergent-misalignment rate, coherence filter or training-stage analysis. One model only.

missing.what: Instructed-hack compliance per grader version (untrained 62.3%; quote+explain 13%; quote whole 41%; PASS-only 7.2%). Also writing-grader results: 48.7% vs 47.6% on writing, 45% vs 60% on code. Not emergent misalignment, but needed to interpret r2–r4.

record.verdict_notes: The record treats grader training as a V2-style narrow fine-tune and reward hacking as the misalignment measure. Neither matches the claim, which concerns broad misaligned answers after training on producing narrow bad outputs. The r2–r4 condition appears mislabelled: the 60% baseline matches the instructed setting.

versions.untested_parts: The study trains models to grade coding submissions, not to write insecure code for unsuspecting users; it does not compare that training with secure-code or class-framed insecure-code fine-tunes.
Tests reward-hack grading and reward-hacking behavior, not bad medical or financial advice, number sequences, or broad misaligned answers such as praising authoritarianism or giving malicious advice.
No narrow in-context-only condition is tested.
The study uses SFT, not reinforcement learning.

The mechanistic experiment uses one grading direction from one grader-training condition and measures behavior under an explicit hacking instruction; it does not test a shared mechanism across fine-tunes for naturally arising behavior.
No inoculation framing or brief benign retraining mitigation is tested.
Only Qwen3-14B is studied. There is no size sweep, coherence-filter analysis, or training-stage sweep; seed results are reported for the non-coding evaluation.

rows.subject: 11 Qwen3-14B grader models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned to grade coding submissions for reward hacks; evaluated writing code without a hack instruction.
rows.measure: Rate of code answers classified as hacks
rows.baseline: 0% for the untrained model without the hack instruction
rows.value: 7 of 28,160 answers; at most one per model
rows.locator: Experiment 1 – Does grading hacks teach hacking?
rows.note: The author describes this as on par with untrained models. The aggregate covers 11 grader models.
rows.check: Measures reward hacking after grader training, not broad misalignment after a narrow fine-tune of the kind V2 names. V7 is also wrong: this is not effect size or robustness of emergent misalignment. Value and baseline (0% untrained without instruction; 7/28,160) are correctly read.
